ELI5: How is linear algebra used to graph in 3 dimensions?

Vectors allow you to determine 3d space effectively.

tldr; vectors are awesome.

If you remember back in grade school when you learned about coordinate geometry, you'll recall that you can draw lines with different slopes, lengths, etc. In linear algebra, we represent that graph that you drew on with something called a Basis. All a Basis is, is essentially a rule-set of how far a line can go in either direction (x, y, z, etc.). Generally, these are represented as a vector. For example, the standard basis, the basis you learned in middle school, is just the vectors (1,0) & (0,1). The first is for the x-direction, and the second for the y-direction. These vectors are super unique, because you'll notice that either one is not dependent on the other. As in, I cannot make the y-direction out of any combinations of the x-directions.

Now extending into 3 dimensional space, the same rules apply. If we're looking at just a standard 3D graph, the standard basis is (1,0,0), (0,1,0), & (0,0,1)--each corresponding the an axis. Now for any 3 dimensional graph equation that you can think of that is real and doesn't use imaginary numbers, or any funky stuff, finding a basis for it is pretty trivial. (There are procedures that you can learn in linear algebra that make this into a sort of algorithm to follow). Then, there is a magic rule called the Change of Basis that will switch your equation's vectors into vectors of the form s(1,0,0)+t(0,1,0)+c(0,0,1) where s,t,c are just scalar multiples of the original standard basis vectors, and they will tell you how far in either direction to go.

The really fun part comes in when you apply these principles to n-dimensions, which is seriously nearly as easy as 3 dimensions. That's why I love Linear Algebra--it allowed you to calculate really cool stuff in huge dimensions with no hope of visualizing it, but still yielding a correct answer. Another really cool aspect is that those bases I talked about are not super special. I could just as easily represent your equation set in 3 dimensions with a basis that was created from a 5 dimensional equation! You can also start to get really funky bases that severely limit how the transformation looks i.e., could shrink down most any equation into super small vectors, etc.

I hope this explains it well!

Linear algebra is the branch of math that deals with the study of lines, planes and subspaces. The most fundamental component of this study are the lines. Kind of like how atoms are the cornerstone of chemistry, lines are the cornerstone of linear algebra.

Lines can be described in a few ways, most notably, they can be categorized as scalars and vectors. Vectors are distinct from scalars in that they have directionality. For instance, "5 miles per hour" would be considered a scalar because it tells you the magnitude of the distance, but not its direction. Thus, you can't move in 3D space effectively. So, a vector would be equivalent to "5 miles per hour, East".
